impacts.caseName: Trustees of Columbia University v. Gen Digital Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to methods for detecting anomalous program executions by comparing function calls in an emulator to a model of function calls are abstract under step one of the Alice framework, and whether damages based on foreign sales were properly awarded.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated a $185 million jury verdict for Columbia, holding that the asserted claims of the '322 and '115 patents are abstract at Alice step one and remanding for further proceedings on step two eligibility. The court also held that the district court erred in permitting damages based on Norton's sales to customers outside the United States, and reversed the contempt finding against Norton's counsel Quinn Emanuel.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens defendants' ability to challenge cybersecurity and software patents under § 101, and limits patentees from recovering damages on extraterritorial sales, reducing potential exposure for global technology companies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the software and cybersecurity space face heightened risk that their claims will be deemed abstract, potentially undermining the enforceability and value of existing patent portfolios.

impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly granted judgment as a matter of law that Teva's headache patents claiming humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies for treating headache were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity, reinstating a jury verdict that Eli Lilly willfully infringed Teva's headache patents covering the use of humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies. The court found the district court applied incorrect legal standards for written description and enablement in the context of antibody genus claims with disclosed prior-art methods.
impacts.positiveImplications: Bolsters pharmaceutical patent holders' ability to enforce genus claims for biologics where the specification discloses known methods and at least one species, strengthening patent protection for blockbuster antibody therapies like Teva's Ajovy.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar manufacturers face greater difficulty in challenging the validity of broad biologic patent claims, potentially delaying market entry and increasing litigation costs.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether there was a legally sufficient evidentiary basis to support the jury's finding that each of the four asserted trade secrets was protectable under California law, and whether the named inventors' patent claims were invalid for failure to name the correct inventor.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of JMOL on trade secret misappropriation claims, holding that the plaintiff failed to prove the asserted trade secrets were protectable because the underlying ideas were generally known in the field. The court also reversed the denial of JMOL on patent invalidity and vacated the permanent injunction, reasonable royalty, and exemplary damages, while affirming liability on a trademark counterfeiting claim.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides defendants with stronger grounds to challenge trade secret claims where the alleged secrets involve generally known information, reinforcing the requirement that trade secret plaintiffs must prove genuine secrecy with specificity.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret holders face a higher evidentiary bar to sustain jury verdicts, and companies relying on trade secret protection for commercially valuable know-how must ensure robust documentation distinguishing their secrets from publicly available knowledge.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly granted summary judgment of noninfringement based on extraterritoriality and rejection of a doctrine of equivalents theory, and whether it properly struck the patentee's damages expert theories.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's grant of summary judgment on extraterritoriality grounds, finding genuine disputes of material fact as to whether Intel's accused multicore processor operations occurred domestically. The court affirmed the rejection of VLSI's doctrine of equivalents theory and the striking of certain damages theories for inadequate disclosure during discovery.
impacts.positiveImplications: Clarifies that extraterritoriality-based noninfringement defenses for semiconductor and processor technology require careful factual analysis, giving patentees a stronger basis to argue domestic use even where products are designed or partially manufactured abroad.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies relying on the presumption against extraterritoriality as a defense to infringement may find it harder to obtain summary judgment when accused operations have domestic components.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain claims of the '761 and '700 patents directed to non-uniform constellations, finding they required further Alice step-two analysis, while affirming eligibility for claims of the '509 and '922 patents that recited specific technical implementations. The court affirmed the jury's infringement and damages findings, including the admissibility of Constellation's damages expert.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides a roadmap for communications technology patentees to draft claims with sufficient technical specificity to survive § 101 challenges, and affirms that properly supported damages models will be upheld.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies implementing industry-standard communications technologies face continued exposure to patent infringement suits, and the split eligibility outcome creates uncertainty for patent portfolios covering signal processing innovations.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that exclusively licensed manufacturing and commercialization rights but retained the right to sue for infringement and other exclusionary rights has constitutional standing to bring a patent infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patent owner who retains the right to sue for infringement—a right not rendered illusory by the license—possesses a sufficient exclusionary interest to satisfy Article III standing. The court found that the patent owners' retained rights, including approval over sublicenses and assignments, were meaningful exclusionary rights.
impacts.positiveImplications: Clarifies and strengthens the ability of patent owners to enforce patents even after granting broad exclusive licenses, so long as they retain meaningful exclusionary rights such as the right to sue infringers independently.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers will find it harder to dismiss patent suits on standing grounds where the licensor retains litigation rights, potentially increasing the volume of enforceable patent claims they face.

impacts.caseName: Global Tubing LLC v. Tenaris Coiled Tubes LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether genuine disputes of material fact precluded summary judgment on inequitable conduct in obtaining coiled-tubing patents and on a Walker Process antitrust fraud claim based on the same patents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment of inequitable conduct against Tenaris and summary judgment in favor of Tenaris on Global Tubing's Walker Process antitrust claim, finding genuine disputes of material fact on both issues. The court held that the materiality and intent elements of inequitable conduct, and the fraud-on-the-PTO element of the Walker Process claim, required trial.
impacts.positiveImplications: Preserves the viability of Walker Process antitrust claims challenging patents obtained through alleged fraud, giving competitors a tool to challenge patent monopolies in the oil and gas industry.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face increased litigation risk where prior art disclosures during prosecution are disputed, as both inequitable conduct and Walker Process claims may proceed to trial rather than being resolved on summary judgment.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify beyond personal knowledge for purposes of summary judgment, and whether the on-sale bar of 35 U.S.C. § 102(b) requires proof that the prior art sale expressly disclosed the device's functionality.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the pre-AIA on-sale bar, holding that 30(b)(6) deposition testimony is admissible at summary judgment even when the corporate witness lacks personal knowledge, and that the on-sale bar does not require the prior art sale to expressly disclose the device's functionality. The court also held that computer source code constitutes non-hearsay machine commands.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens the ability of accused infringers to use corporate representative testimony and source code evidence to prove on-sale bar invalidity, broadening the evidentiary tools available at summary judgment.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face expanded risk of invalidation under the on-sale bar, as sales of prior art devices need not have disclosed the specific claimed functionality, and corporate witnesses without personal knowledge can testify about historical product sales.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion in excluding a damages expert report for using an improper methodology and then granting summary judgment based on absence of a quantifiable remedy.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the exclusion of Exafer's damages expert report, holding that the district court applied an overly rigid standard in evaluating the expert's reasonable royalty methodology for patents covering virtual network optimization technology. The court vacated summary judgment of no remedy and remanded for further proceedings, including potential reopening of discovery.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides patent plaintiffs greater flexibility in presenting damages theories, signaling that district courts should not exclude expert testimony merely because the methodology is imperfect if it is grounded in accepted principles.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology defendants like Microsoft may face renewed exposure to damages claims previously dismissed on Daubert grounds, increasing litigation costs and settlement pressure.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an ITC respondent may obtain a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) of a refiled declaratory judgment action after it missed the deadline for seeking a stay of its original declaratory judgment action involving the same parties and issues.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that a respondent in an ITC proceeding may not circumvent the statutory deadline for a mandatory stay under § 1659(a)(2) by dismissing its original declaratory judgment action and refiling a new one. The court found this would allow gamesmanship that Congress did not intend.
impacts.positiveImplications: Prevents ITC respondents from manipulating litigation timelines by refiling district court actions to obtain stays, protecting patent holders' ability to pursue parallel enforcement in district court and at the ITC.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC respondents who miss the 30-day stay deadline lose the ability to obtain a mandatory stay of the corresponding district court action, potentially forcing them to litigate on two fronts simultaneously.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in pharmaceutical composition patents refers to a pH measured at a standard temperature in the field, and whether Actelion was barred from asserting infringement under the doctrine of equivalents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding of no literal infringement and no infringement under the doctrine of equivalents for Actelion's epoprostenol formulation patents. The court agreed that 'a pH of 13 or higher' is measured at the field-standard temperature of 25°C, and that Actelion was barred from asserting equivalents due to prosecution history estoppel.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides clarity for generic drug manufacturers on how pH-related claim terms are interpreted in ANDA litigation, supporting generic entry for hypertension treatments.
impacts.negativeImplications: Pharmaceutical patentees face narrower claim scope when specifications and prosecution history tie quantitative parameters to standard measurement conditions, limiting both literal and equivalents-based infringement theories.

impacts.caseName: National Veterans Legal Services Program v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly approved a $125 million class action settlement of claims that the federal judiciary overcharged PACER users, and whether incentive awards to class representative nonprofit organizations were permissible.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed approval of a $125 million settlement in a nationwide class action challenging excessive PACER fees charged to access court records. The court upheld the settlement terms, attorneys' fees, and incentive awards to the three nonprofit class representatives, rejecting objections regarding subject matter jurisdiction and Supreme Court precedent on incentive awards.
impacts.positiveImplications: Validates the settlement framework for large-scale government overcharge class actions and confirms that nonprofit class representatives may receive incentive awards, providing certainty for future class action settlements involving government fees.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC correctly found that Apple's importation and sale of Apple Watches with blood oxygen measurement features violated Section 337 of the Tariff Act by infringing Masimo's wearable pulse oximetry patents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's determination that Apple violated Section 337 and upheld the limited exclusion order barring importation of infringing Apple Watch models. The court found no error in the Commission's domestic industry determination, patent validity rulings, or infringement findings related to Masimo's wearable blood oxygen measurement patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens patent holders' ability to enforce patents at the ITC against major consumer electronics companies, demonstrating that exclusion orders remain a powerful remedy for protecting patented wearable health technologies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies incorporating health-monitoring features into consumer devices face significant import exclusion risk, potentially requiring costly design-arounds and disrupting product availability in the U.S. market.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB's obviousness determination was supported by substantial evidence where the Board relied on prior art without adequately explaining the motivation to combine, and whether a non-party to district court litigation may file IPR petitions on behalf of or in coordination with a time-barred party.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the Board's finding that all challenged claims of FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent were unpatentable as obvious, holding that the Board failed to adequately explain the motivation to combine the prior art references. The court declined to review the Board's denial of FedEx's motion to terminate the IPR based on the alleged time-bar issue.
impacts.positiveImplications: Reinforces that the PTAB must provide thorough articulation of motivation to combine in obviousness determinations, protecting patent holders from insufficiently reasoned invalidation of logistics and IoT patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: IPR petitioners face stricter requirements to demonstrate motivation to combine prior art, potentially making it harder to invalidate patents through inter partes review proceedings.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC correctly determined that Tineco's redesigned wet-dry surface cleaning devices did not infringe Bissell's patents, and whether Bissell established a technical domestic industry for the asserted patents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's determination in full, upholding both the finding that Tineco's redesigned products did not infringe Bissell's surface cleaning apparatus patents and the finding that Bissell satisfied the technical domestic industry requirement. The exclusion order against Tineco's original infringing products was maintained.
impacts.positiveImplications: Confirms that effective product redesigns can escape ITC exclusion orders, providing importers with a clear path to continue market participation after adverse Section 337 findings.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders may find it difficult to extend ITC exclusion orders to redesigned products, potentially limiting the long-term effectiveness of Section 337 enforcement actions.
